Western Postal Employees
On section 1-Salaries of certain post office employees who were dismissed and reemployed.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: I might draw the attention of the committee to the fact that the bill is in similar terms to the resolution as amended by the house yesterday, and which was fully discussed the other day. If hon. members will compare section 1 of the bill, which is the only section, with the resolution adopted yesterday, they will find that it is in exact conformity with the resolution as adopted.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: Yesterday when the minister was discussing the resolution upon which this bill is founded, he indicated that there was a certain procedure to be followed. I think he said that an appointee of the Civil Service Commission and an expert of the department would be appointed to check the matter over and to determine the manner in which the terms of the bill should be applied, but I see no such provision in the bill.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
There is no such provision
in the bill, because I did not think it necessary to insert it. If, however, the committee regard it as necessary, it will be an easy matter to add a second clause to the ball.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Speaking for myself, I
would say unquestionably that it ought to be in the bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: I do not know whether my hon. friend was in the house yesterday when the Postmaster General made his statement. He indicated then the method that would be taken to ascertain what remuneration, if any, was due to certain of the employees of the department. As I recall it, an officer of the Post Office department and one from the Civil Service Commission were to cooperate with the postmaster at Winnipeg in making a report to the minister. I do not know whether my hon. friend1 really feels that that ought to be incorporated as a section of the act. It is purely an administrative matter, and I think that the word of the ministry in a matter of that kind ought to be sufficient; there is no desire on the part of the government to deal with the matter in any unfair way. But to put a purely administrative clause dealing with detail into a bill which merely provides for repaying men what is owing to them seems to me to be loading the bill perhaps unduly.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
May I draw the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that this bill contains the proviso, "notwithstanding

anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act." In other words, so far as this matter is concerned the Civil Service Act is repealed or entirely superseded. We have set up under the Civil Service Act certain machinery to deal with the civil service of Canada, and therefore inasmuch as you are eliminating the Civil Service Act entirely from this matter -by the way, may I interject here this suggestion, that a lot of these men were placed in their positions in the Winnipeg post office without reference to the Civil Service Commission, after they were reemployed in contravention of the terms of the Civil Service Act-

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: All the appoinments were made by the Civil Service Commission.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: My hon. friend is in error.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: The only exception was the age limit.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: I think it will be found that I am absolutely correct in what I am saying. Therefore I contend that this bill should contain a clause setting out the manner in which this extraordinary procedure is to be carried out; because we must admit it is not the ordinary procedure. There should be recognition of the Civil Service Commission and its knowledge of the technique in this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
May I say
to my hon. friend that to be logical I think any reference to the Civil Service Commission should be left out, I agree entirely with him that these men were reemployed notwithstanding the Civil Service Act. When the original resolution was before the house I gathered from what the right hon. leader of the opposition said that the men had been reinstated under an order in council passed by virtue of the War Measures Act, and that that was the reason why the civil service law had been ignored. I have since discovered that the order in council was not passed under the War Measures Act at all, but as a matter of fact it was simply an arbitrary act on the part of the government of the day. Now, all this measure proposes is that where

Western Postal Employees
those men have been employed on a certain class of work at a lower rate of wages than is paid to other employees in that class, they shall be paid the difference in remuneration due to them on that score.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: Should not the right hon. gentleman use the word " reemployed " rather than " reinstated "?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: Yes, instead of " reinstated " I should have used the word "reemployed." I gathered from the discussion when the resolution was originally introduced that we were practically in agreement on the question of paying the men the difference between what they are or were actually earning in accordance with the rate of wages the positions carry and what they are or were being paid. The only difference between us was whether that extra payment should.be retroactive. The house having passed the resolution and adopted the principle of the bill, the only question which remains is that of the method by which we shall ascertain what is due to the men. The Minister of Justice says it would be difficult to frame a clause setting out this feature which is wholly administrative. Therefore I should hope that hon. gentlemen opposite would accept the Postmaster General's statement to the house as to the method he proposes, with the obligation of course on his part of being responsible to the house for carrying out matters in accordance with that method. I should think this should be sufficient.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
May I ask the Prime
Minister if the bill as now drawn does provide for retroactive pay? I was not here when the discussion took place on the resolution. I understand from reading the discussion that my hon. leader, who is absent to-day, took the ground that he would not agree to a proposal which provided for retroactive pay. Does the modified proposal provide for retroactive pay?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite right. The only difference between us is that the government maintains that these men where they have actually performed the work should be paid for it at the current rates, whether it relates to the future or to the past. I gathered at the time the measure was under discussion that the leader of the opposition did not wish to go to the length of paying for work done in the past, although it had not been paid for at the current rates. I had rather hoped that in the interval my hon. friends opposite had changed their views. On that point there is still a difference between us.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: Will the Postmaster General kindly say how much money this measure will involve?

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: On a previous occasion I said $123,000. Since then I have been able to go into it minutely and I do not think the cost will exceed $100,000. Since the committee sat last we have ascertained that the Winnipeg authorities have an absolutely correct record of all the men reemployed and the positions they were put in and as they graduated-if I may use that term from one class to another, and the difference in the rates of salaries, and so forth. That is why yesterday I suggested that two persons be appointed, one representing the department itself, the administrative end, and the other the Civil Service Commission, and that these two men go to Winnipeg. Then with the information they already had and the information they would get in Winnipeg, they could take the list of 9fii men, go over it in detail, and work out each individual case. Under the system there may be some who, having come in later, will not be entitled to anything; there are others who came in at the first and certainly will be entitled to be considered under this bill. It is a matter that will take some time to work out. Working off and on, I think the two gentlemen I have in mind could complete their task in about two months. As I say, they would have to go to Winnipeg, get the balance of the information there and work it out from both ends, from the departmental end here and from the Winnipeg end. By that system it can be done.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: Has the minister any clear conception as to how this can be worked out? For instance, these men, had they stayed in the service, would have got promotion. Not having stayed in the service, but being reemployed, some of them later got promotion. How are you going to average the graduation between those two promotions? It is absolutely impossible.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: That will have to be worked out from the very first moment the men were taken back, dealing with it year by year and taking into consideration what promotion they were entitled to and got during that time, and also what extra amount of money those promotions brought to them. It will take some considerable time to work out the details.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
The minister does not get my point. Supposing there had been no strike, and these men had stayed in the service, automatically they would have got promotion, would they not.

Western Postal Employees

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: That is one step. Then you reemploy them and they get promotion along another line; how are you going to readjust those two Lines?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: My hon. friend, I am afraid, is confusing the present bill with the original resolution. As originally introduced there was all the difficulty my hon. friend sees in making the assessment, if I may use that term, because it would have put the men in the same position they would have been in if they had not gone on strike. All the present bill does is to take into account the work a man is doing or has done in the particular position occupied and if he is being or has been paid less than other men in similar positions, then he shall be given the difference.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: The Prime Minister does not get my point. How is he going to get at what they would have earned?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: It is not what they would have earned; it is what they have actually earned. For instance, take a man who is a sorter. He is working with a lot of sorters in the office. Let us suppose he is one of the men who went out on strike. When he was reemployed he was reemployed as a postal helper, and he 'has been receiving the wages of a postal helper, notwithstanding that he has been doing the work of a sorter. All this bill provides is that when that sort of thing happens, or has happened, the man who has been doing a sorter's work shall be paid as though he were entitled to sorter's wages from the time that he was engaged on sorter's work. That is all.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: That would be all right from the start; but how are you going to decide two or three years afterwards what position he might have been in?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
What counts
is what he has actually done in that time.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
There should be added to the bill a clause elaborating the system under which the money is to be distributed. As the bill is drawn now the Civil Service Act has no bearing on it at all; the Civil Service Commission is practically wiped out. There is no one left to administer the fund but the Post Office Department and the Postmaster General. He may do it in any way he sees fit and there is no check whatever on him. There are ninety-six men to be provided for, and with the commission wiped out, as it is by the first clause of the bill, the matter
[Mrt McGibbon.]
is in the hands of the Postmaster General who may deal with the fund as he sees fit. In my opinion the scheme should be elaborated by a new clause; it is entirely too open at the present time. If the scheme is to be worked out under the supervision of the Post Office Department and the Civil Service Commission, let us so state; but as the matter stands the Civil Service Commission will not be appealed to at all. It will be purely a matter of departmental administration by the Post Office Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: How does my hon. friend reconcile his position this afternoon with reference to this matter with the attitude he took a few days ago when he urged us to put in a special vote for certain postal workers?

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
I named the postal
worker and the amount in each case, and if that is done here it gets over the difficulty.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
I have just had the bill presented to me and so far as I can see it does not affect the principle of the argument which has already taken place on this question not only this session but on the previous occasion as well. There is no doubt, from the terms of the bill, that this legislation involves retroactive payments to these postal workers. In other words, any striker who was reemployed-not reinstated-after the strike had been settled will now be entitled to claim salary for the work he performed from the date of reemployment until the present moment. That is a correct statement. I am opposed to the retroactive character of this bill for the reasons I have already stated. These men went out on a sympathetic strike and according to some they had grievances; but having seen the gravity of ithe situation in which they placed themselves they were taken back into the service. Now that does not justify any government in paying to them salaries for such services as they were willing and anxious to render at that time; they were reemployed as postal helpers and they went back on that understanding, and on that basis they should still be dealt with.
I do not think there is any great merit in what the leader of the opposition says with respect to the way in which the fund will be dealt with, but I do think that some consideration should be given to the principle involved. I cannot, for one, take the position that civil servants in the class of these workers should have the right to strike and thereby upset the whole business of the country; I should as soon expect the police or the army or the navy to take that attitude and go on strike. And if this bill is passed as it stands a precedent will be established and

C.N.R.-Purchase of Alberta Railways
other public servants will feel entitled to similar treatment under circumstances of a like character. Not long ago I read of the strike that took place in England in 1919 on the part of the policemen, and they certainly were not reinstated in the service; and the same principle applies here. I am opposed to the retroactive principle involved in this bill. If these men wish now to get the seniority to which they are entitled I am willing and anxious that they shall be given it, but the retroactive feature I must oppose.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

subtopic: AGREEMENT FOR THE PURCHASE OF ALBERTA RAILWAYS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 14, consideration of the motion of Hon. Charles A. Dunning (Minister of Railways and Canals) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee on Bill No. 71, to incorporate the Northern Alberta Railways Compaq', and respecting the Canadian National Railway Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

subtopic: AGREEMENT FOR THE PURCHASE OF ALBERTA RAILWAYS
speechtext:
When the house adjourned last night I was pointing out that the Alberta government had offered the Peace River railway to the Canadian National Railways. I notice that I stated the price offered as $14,000,000; I should have said $16,500,000. This was in 1926. Previous to that time the Canadian Pacific Railway had operated the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia and Central Canada railways under an operating arrangement with the Alberta government. They claim to be losing money on the operation of these railways but the Alberta government declined to enter into a lease for a further period of time with the Canadian Pacific Railway; instead they appointed Mr. Callaghan manager of the railways and made a joint traffic arrangement with the Canadian National Railways. There was a very strong feeling in Peace River and in certain sections of Alberta that the Canadian National Railways should get the preference in connection with the purchase of these railways on condition that the offers were alike, in case offers were received from both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway for their purchase. A large number 78594-160}
of members of the legislature took this view. The Grand Prairie district in Peace River was strongly in favour of the Canadian National, the town of Peace River was favourable to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the district north of Peace' River, where I reside myself, was somewhat neutral. The people there thought it was up to the Alberta government to get the best price possible.
So far as I am concerned, I have always favoured the acquisition of these railways by the Canadian National Railways because in the first place I am rather favourable to national ownership as against private ownership of railways; and in the second place the Canadian National was in a much better position geographically through the location of its railways and could give the Peace River such service as the Canadian Pacific Railway could not provide without a large expenditure in extensions westward. The Canadian National Railways could give Peace River entry into Vancouver and Prince Rupert with the construction of from 200 to 500 miles of railway, whereas the Canadian Pacific Railway could not do so without building between 600 and 1,200 miles of railway. I have felt all along that if the Canadian National purchased the Alberta railways they were much more likely to work out a solution of the problem so far as the coast outlet was concerned in the near future than was the Canadian Pacific. Between May 3, 1926, and September 17, 1928, a number of offers were made in connection with these railways. The Premier of Alberta offered the Minister of Railways the Central Canada, the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia and the Pembina railways for about $16,500,000. On November 11, 1927, Mr. Hungerford wrote Mr. Brownlee offering $17,200,000, in round figures, on behalf of the Canadian National Railways, but that offer was turned down by the Alberta government. On November 13, 1927, Mr. Brownlee suggested to the Minister of Railways the possibility of a joint offer, because the Alberta government were not satisfied with the offer of the Canadian National Railways and would not accept it, suggesting that a better offer might result through joint action of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. A joint offer was submitted on January 16, 1928, offering somewhat better terms than had been offered by the Canadian National Railways, but this was still unsatisfactory to the Alberta government. On September 17, 1928, the Canadian Pacific bought the road, including the Alberta Great Waterways, for $25,000,000, and on November 26.

1928, Sir Henry Thornton, notified Mr. Beatty that the Canadian National Railways would participate in the arrangement on a fifty-fifty basis.
It has been felt in Peace river and the view has been expressed in other parts of the country that between the Canadian National Railways and the government a good opportunity was lost to get hold of the Peace river railways; others have thought the Alberta government somewhat unreasonable in their demands, but I do not believe that to be the case, because the price of the Alberta railways went up steadily after 1926. The reason for that increase is shown in the speech delivered by Hon. V. W. Smith in the Alberta legislature during the last session of that body. He said:
The first full year of government operation, that of 1927, resulted in a .net operating surplus for all the northern railways of $303,786.63, as against an operating deficit of $188,655.34 in the previous year. This was regarded by the government as a very satisfactory outcome of its policy in assuming control of all the northern roads. The results obtained for the year 1928, however, have been even more satisfactory than those of 1927, and it is gratifying for me to be able to announce that the total operating surplus derived from all the northern railways for the year 1928 is $810,209.41.
That represents an improvement in earning of almost $1,000,000 in two years, and that is why the Alberta government held out for a good price. That is also the reason why the Canadian Pacific Railway came back and finally bought the roads, because after all n-ot much more than a sixth of the land lying close to these railways has been developed, and yet during the last year of government operation the income was almost sufficient to pay not only the operating charges but the fixed charges as well.
Yesterday' the hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. McRae) said he did not see how any member from the prairie provinces could support this agreement, because it .might put the Peace River country in the position occupied by the three western provinces before the extension west of the Canadian Northern and other railways. At page 2501 of Hansard the hon. member said:
I cannot see how hon. members from the prairie provinces can support a bill which puts the new settlers of the Peace river district in a position similar to that from which the farmers of Manitoba freed themselves more than a generation ago.
That position has to be stated generally in this way: The Canadian Pacific Railway had control and the settlers could not get what they wanted in the way of extensions or railway service, but after the Grand Trunk

Pacific and the Canadian Northern were built that private monopoly was broken up. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that if parliament turns down this bill and does not allow the Canadian National Railways to participate in this scheme, we will be putting the Peace River country in exactly the position occupied by the western provinces some twenty or twenty-five years ago. Because of that fact I was very glad to learn that the Canadian National Railways had decided to go in and help develop that country, because I do not believe this parliament would ratify the construction of another line north, duplicating the present road.
What we want this parliament to do is to take care of the development of that country and build a railway west towards the Pacific coast. The Canadian National Railways could give us an outlet to Vancouver and Prince Rupert without any tremendous expenditure, and if someone comes along with a railway from Stewart we will have three separate outlets. Because of these facts I intend to support this bill.

As I understand them, the advantages of the joint ownership scheme are about as follows:	We will have in the Peace River
country, through the cooperation of the railways, an absence of destructive competition in the building of railways. That means that we should be able to keep away from wrong locations and duplication such as we have had in many parts of the prairie provinces. I think it was demonstrated two years ago that by properly laying out the railways in the Peace River country we would have 6,000 economic acres of land to every mile of railway as against 5,000 acres in the prairie provinces. Another advantage is that we will have a one-line haul to every point touched by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railways throughout Canada, and of course we will get away from any private monopoly.

The second criticism is that of the acquisition jointly of these lines by the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific Railways. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) has recited, not unfairly, the circumstances leading up to the position in which we are now placed. I do not criticize the government of Alberta, because, as owners of the lines, they had a perfect right to negotiate and to do the best they could. I might, conceivably, criticize the way they carried on those negotiations, but it was their own business, and I acknowledge their right to do it their own way. On the other hand, I hardly think it fair that the Peace River country should be circularized, through the newspapers and otherwise, with Statements regarding this government, and its actions with respect to the Peace River railway. Many of these statements have been distinctly contrary to the facts, and I know the hon. member for Peace River would not himself be responsible for the misrepresentations and, in some cases, the absolute falsehoods which have been indulged in, as is illustrated by a copy of the Grande Prairie Herald, which I hold in my hand. The main insinuation is that in some way Sir Henry Thornton was prevented by this government from offering for these railways as much as they were worth to the Canadian National system. In reply to all such insinuations and statements I can only say that Sir Henry Thornton was placed in exactly the same position in connection with the negotiations for the acquisition of these lines as he was in the case of all the other acquisitions, bills for the authorization of which will be before parliament. That is to say, he was given an absolutely free hand to negotiate, in order to reach, if possible, an arrangement which he, as the chief railway executive, could recommend to this government and which would be satisfactory to the vendors in each case. Having reached that point, the next step was to come to the government in order to have the purchase negotiations and tentative arrangements approved. Sir Henry Thornton was at no time prevented, directly or indirectly, by this government from offering for the Alberta railways what in his judgment they were worth to the Canadian National system. I

say this to dispose of that point once and for all.
With regard to the criticism as to the joint acquisition, may I say that the suggestion that an offer be made jointly by both the great railways came to me first by a telegram from Premier Brownlee of Alberta. Being disappointed with the last offer made by the Canadian National Railways independently, Premier Brownlee wired me expressing the view that possibly more satisfactory terms could be secured by both railways acting jointly. At that time I did not have much faith in any result coming about from such a step, but in response to his request I got the two railways together and suggested that an examination should be made of the situation from that point of view. The result was a slightly more favourable offer by the two railways jointly than had been made by the Canadian National individually. As the hon. member for Peace River has said, the joint offer was declined and matters rested there for some time until, finally, the Canadian Pacific Railway made a much larger offer, but a proviso was attached to that offer that the Canadian National Railways should be invited to participate on a fifty-fifty basis in the acquisition of the properties if they so desired.

The house in committee on Bill No. 166, to amend an act respecting the construction of a Canadian National railway line between Grand Mere and East Burrills, in the province of Quebec-Mr. Dunning-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Power to construct and complete line described in schedule.

I think the minister might
give some explanation to the committee as to the largely increased cost in this particular case.

My hon. friend remembers, of course, the discussion in the railway committee, but the house generally is not aware of that. When the bill was before the house previously, some question was raised, I think by the leader of the opposition, as to whether, in view of the high cost, it would be possible for the Grand Mere-East Burrills project to earn interest upon the outlay; whether it was economically sound. Since then I have had that question carefully investigated, and I find that on the basis of presently existing traffic the economies effected will be equivalent to 7i per cent upon the total cost, inclusive of the increase provided for in this bill. The section of the railway referred to is one of the busiest sections of the Canadian National system, and the traffic can be expected to increase as time goes on and, consequently, to produce an even greater return upon the investment.
The two causes for the increased cost in this case were the increased cost of right of way and the increased cost of the grading due to a very much larger quantity of material to be moved. Quoting from the engineer's report:
Over one mile in length of the line was through the town of Sliawinigan Falls, about in the middle of which provision was made for a yard requiring more than normal width of right of way. Isot only did it cost more to buy the right of way through Shawinigan Falls -but the whole right of way proved to-be over double that figured on. In practi-

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
cally every ease a process of law had to be resorted to in order to settle the prices paid. Presumably one reason why excessive prices were asked was because the railway was not wanted by the farmer through whose land it passed as he would get no service additional to what he already had.
The increase in quantities of material required to he. moved was due to the nature of the material itself. Generally speaking the overburden on top of the rock which only outcropped in a few places on the line, was a stratum of sandy material about eight or nine feet in depth under which was brown or blue clay. In most cases this lower material was blue clay of a very wet and soft consistency, which when disturbed at all became unstable. This instability in cuttings caused sliding or sloughing-in of the materal into the cuttings, and where embankments were made from it, it slid or squashed out. This condition varied considerably in individual cases. Some of the material was so bad that the embankments could not be made from it, and other material had to be brought from a greater distance to take its place.
A description of the largest and worst cutting will give an example of how this material acted. The cutting in question was located about a mile from the west end of the line and immediately west of a rock tunnel on the line. It was about nine hundred feet in length and at the deepest part was sixty feet in depth. The material was so soft after having been dug with a steam shovel that when dumped out of the cars used for hauling it, it ran 'like thin porridge and proved utterly worthless for filling material. In fact, substantially all of it was deposited off a few feet of trestle built alongside a gully and it imme-diatey flowed or moved from this gully until it reached the St. Maurice river about a mile away.
We estimate that by reducing the gradient to one-half the existing gradient and by doubling the load behind a standard locomotive, the economies effected will be sufficient on the basis of existing traffic to pay 7i per cent on the whole cost of the undertaking.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
