I have already referred to the advice of the experts who say that it does not appear that the acquisition of these lines could ever become profitable to the Dominion, and notwithstanding this the National Railways are acquiring the property. In the face of the financial obligations to which reference was made yesterday, I submit to the minister .that this is a very questionable action on the part of the National Railways and, in the light of this report, disposes us to scrutinize with greater care than we have done in the past the suggestions of the railway. I say that with regret, because I have said to the minister on two or three occasions, and said it gladly, that we have been reposing tremendous confidence in the management of the National Railways in any recommendations they make. But I cannot reconcile-

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: I do hope my hon. friend will turn the searchlight with equal force on each one of the succeeding bills which have to do with purchases. I think it is proper and right that he should.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: I am picking this bill out because I know that there is an adverse report, and if there are adverse reports in regard to the others the fact ought to be disclosed.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: I will discuss the word "adverse" later.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
I am quite willing to leave it at that. But let me repeat what I was saying. We have received the recommendations of the management of the Canadian

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
National Railways with a great deal of favour in this house in recent years, and I should like to voice this opinion, that the National Railways management must be very careful in recommending a purchase of this character in the teeth of a report of the nature to which I have referred. I submit to the minister that there are features of this purchase, disclosed in this report, which make me very doubtful indeed of the wisdom of proceeding with the purchase.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has discussed this bill. This is an undertaking which dates back many years. I will not go over the history of it because I do not wish to delay the house. But I may observe that in 1882'Sir Charles Tupper was Minister of Railways while Sir Hector Langevin was chief of the province of Quebec, and the latter advocated and obtained the authority of parliament for the construction of a branch line of the Intercolonial railway from Matapedia towards Gaspe along the north shore of the baie de Chaleur. Parliament acquiesced in the proposal and the undertaking was commenced by the Dominion government as the construction of a branch line of the Intercolonial. The first twenty miles were accordingly built under contracts given by the Department of Railways. Unfortunately, about the same time the legislature of Quebec had incorporated a local company called the Baie de Chaleur Railway Company, with which was connected Mr. Robitaille, a former representative of Bonaventure in this house, Mr. Riopelle, another member of this house and a former representative of that county, and Mr. C. N. Armstrong, a noted promoter in the province of Quebec. These gentlemen induced1 the Dominion government to give up the undertaking and to hand it over to the local company known as the Baie de Chaleur Railway Company and composed of those whom I have named. The misfortunes of the people of Gaspe and Bonaventure commenced from that time in 1884. The people there had witnessed, and had contributed to, the construction of the Intercolonial railway which runs through the Matapedia valley in my constituency and crosses the river Matapedia into New Brunswick and the maritime provinces. They who had contributed their share to the construction of this railway, linking up Quebec with the maritime provinces, were left to one side and this undertaking of the local company was carried on purely through subsidies granted by the Dominion government and by the legislature of Quebec. So long as the subsidies lasted the
undertaking was carried on as best it could be, with the help of the municipalities and of the farmers, who gave right of way without compensation. As a matter of fact many of those farmers are unpaid to this day. When I had the honour of being elected for that constituency in 1900 I found the railway stranded at Caplin, eighty miles from Matapedia, the railway subsidies exhausted, and the road not operated for six months of the year during the winter. I therefore undertook to secure the consent and approbation of the parliament of Canada to extend railway facilities to the people of that peninsula who were among the oldest settlers of Canada, descendants of people who settled when Jacques Cartier discovered Canada. I sought to give them some of the benefits which we had been providing for the rest of the country in a matter of railway accommodation. The hon. the Speaker (Mr. Lemieux) and myself have witnessed during thirty-two sessions the construction of continental and branch line railways all over Canada and now we merely ask for approval for one simple proposal, namely, that this branch line, running 200 miles from Matapedia to Gaspe,, connecting with the Intercolonial railway, and receiving all its business from the Canadian National Railways-it can do business with no other railway-be utilized as a branch line, as it was intended to be regarded the day it was constructed. With the aid of subsidies voted in 1901 the line was extended to Paspebiac, one hundred miles from Matapedia. His Honour the Speaker had the distinction at that time of being the representative of probably the only constituency in Canada without a mile of railway, and naturally he undertook to bring about the extension of that line as originally planned by those great leaders of public opinion, Sir Charles Tupper and1 Sir Hector Langevin, and later by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He endeavoured to have it extended to Gaspe. The charter was passed, the usual subsidies were voted, and in addition a subsidy of $250,000 was granted by the house towards the construction of numerous iron and steel bridges across the river emptying into baie de Chaleur. An English company undertook to build the railway and completed the work in 1911, when it had reached Gaspe. Shortly after that, in 1914, this house passed what was known as the Branch Lines Act, a measure which authorized the government of Canada to acquire every branch line of 200 miles connecting with the Canadian Government Railways, at that time largely the Intercolonial railway. They took over a dozen lines in the maritime provinces and
C.N.R.-Branch 1/ines

in Quebec, but this railway was left to one side. In 1914 the war came on, and that was put forward as an excuse for doing nothing. Nor was anything done until 1921, when the Liberal party returned to office and the argument was again taken up by the people of these two counties asking that this railway should form part and parcel of the Canadian National Railways and be given the same treatment as had been meted out to others throughout the country.
Now I am speaking not for one party but for the whole population of that district; I am representing the views of all political parties, religions and creeds. And I am glad to know that I am speaking also on behalf of the Conservative party, because two years ago, on the 2nd of August, 1926, the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen, who then undertook the campaign which led him to his defeat in the month of September, opened that campaign in my constituency at Carleton.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
That was the cause of
the defeat?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Yes. He was accompanied by Mr. Patenaude, his first lieutenant in Quebec and they were ferried across from Bathurst in New Brunswick by Mr. Angus McLean in a tug, landing at Carleton. Fortunately a correspondent of the Canadian Press accompanied Mr. Meighen on that occasion and reported his remarks which are to be found in the Montreal Gazette of August 2, 1926, and I desire merely to quote that part of his address referring to this railway situation. He congratulated the people on the progress they had made in that hard country, where they have long winter seasons and large families to keep up, and after referring to the fact that from these two constituencies 1,200 boys were sent to the front during the war, he went on to state:
One could not help realizing that there might be indeed a gratifying development if there could be found a method of extending to this district, as yet relatively thinly populated, something of the help which the Dominion has been able to give to other parts of the Dominion. I know that your resources are many and precious. You have splendid timber resources. You have mineral resources. Your agricultural resources are as yet only tapped. It will be impossible that these will progress as you expect-, unless something is done to help with the transportation of your commodities.
. . . . Iam quite aware that there are difficulties in the way. I never could be convinced that it is not going to mean considerable outlay over a considerable time. But I intend to give sympathetic consideration to this question. I am going, as it were, to put my head into it. I hope to say to the people of this province-I promise I will say to them whenever I occupy the post of Prime Minister by 
the verdict of the people-that whatever is done for any part of the Dominion, the same measure of generosity, the same measure of justice will be given to the province of Quebec and to every part of the province of Quebec.
Some days later he appointed my opponent, Doctor Paquet, as Minister of Health and Soldier's Civil Re-establishment, notwithstanding his campaign at that time which had become notorious. On August 23 Doctor Paquet was sworn in to this portfolio as a member of the Meighen administration, and stated publicly that if within two years this railway situation was not settled and the railway linked up with the Canadian National Railways, he would retire from the House of Commons and resign his portfolio.
Matters went along until 1923, when the Speaker of this house, acting for his constituency and for my own, called upon the government to have this situation investigated by the railway commission. On that occasion I had the honour of accompanying the commission as far as Gaspe; .they were accompanied by their entire staff and spent about three days investigating the situation. In their report is included a statement by Judge McKeown, who spoke on behalf of the commission, confirming the statement made some years previously by Hon. F. B. Carvell when he was chairman of the commission. On July 21, 1920, Mr. Carvell said:
It is, therefore, quite evident that this road is in very much the same position as the branch lines in New Brunswick, excepting that, in my opinion, it goes through a better country as a rule than do the New Brunswick roads. There are more people to patronize it, more business to be done, the road-bed is in better condition, and it offers a better guarantee of business than any of the other branch lines with which we have been dealing during the past three years.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: What year was that?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: What is the hon. member quoting from?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: I am going to quote from Sir Henry's remarks in the railway committee.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Recently?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Yes, when this bill was under consideration. Sir Henry Thornton said:
There are two aspects to this situation. First, the purchase price of the railway as compared with the immediate returns; secondly, the prospects of the railway as an earner in hands which will indicate that an effort will be made to secure the assistance of the people of the Gaspe peninsula in creating traffic and development. That is a situation which always confronts the Canadian National Railway, as a state-owned property, in this sense, that it stands in a somewhat different relationship to the various communities which it serves than does a purely privately-owned company, in that it must give greater regard to the assistance of communities in their development.
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

Now, the principle which underlies the purchase of this property is not much different from the principle we have followed in building branch lines throughout the west for development purposes.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Is the hon. member quoting Sir Henry Thornton?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Yes. Sir Henry continues:
It happened that in this case the railway is already built. In the west the railways were not built, but we were pledged to embark upon new construction, but the underlying principle in each case is to give to each one of the communities a service which offers prospective traffic and an opportunity for the community to develop. As I said, in this case we are purchasing a railway already built, in the west we are building new railways; the principle is naturally pretty much the same.
The hon. member who has just piit a question to me was present in the committee and cross-questioned Sir Henry pretty thoroughly with regard to this matter. That deals with the economic aspect of the question, with which, not being an engineer, I am not familiar. But there is another portion of Sir Henry's remarks which I would like to quote, as follows:
The purchase price is $3,500,000, which was arrived at after negotiations with the trustees, and represents the cost of reproduction now less depreciation less subsidies paid. The Gaspe railways were exploited by Alfred M. Carpenter, at one time proprietor of the Charing Cross bank

That is an error, as Mr. Carpenter never operated the railway. Sir Henry continues:
-which became bankrupt a great many years ago, and the property has since been operated by trustees for the bond holders.
That briefly represents the historical and physical conditions, and I can say that the negotiations were carried on by myself with Sir William Plender, a well known chartered accountant in London, England, who represents the trustees.
After some negotiations with him, it was agreed to purchase the property for $3,500,000, subject to the approval of parliament. That represents 50 cents on the dollar invested.
This territory has, for a long time, suffered from inadequate transportation facilities and, for that reason, has been unable to participate in the development which has taken place elsewhere in Canada The population is an exceedingly thrifty, hardworking population, of the best of our French stock.
It was felt that if the railway fell into hands which would foster development in the peninsula, lend its efforts with the people of the peninsula for development purposes, coupled with the possibilities of a large tourist traffic, that a considerable impetus would be given to development in the Gaspe peninsula, and it was for those reasons that it was thought desirable by the Canadian National Railways to take over the line.
As my time is limited I will not be able to go into this matter much further. The hon.
IMr. Marcil.I
member for Vancouver mentioned a report which was made by the Canadian National railway officials, the last paragraph of which reads as follows:
It does not appear that the acquisition of the Quebec Oriental Railway by the Canadian government could ever become profitable.
There is only one railway official of that opinion, and no matter how important the opinion may be it is merely an opinion and it deals with the future. I have been in the house for thirty-two years and I have heard many false prophecies made by very outstanding men. I was up in the press gallery when it was predicted that the Canadian Pacific Railway would never pay for the grease used in its operation. That prediction was made by some very eminent men, and many other false prophecies have been made in the house.
The Gaspe peninsula has an area of 10,000 square miles. It contains abundant lumber, minerals and other natural products

mines are being developed now for the production of zinc and lead-as well as abundant fisheries. It has a magnificent harbour which is the closest in North America to Liverpool, being only four days' sail from Gaspe. This harbour was large enough to shelter in 1914 the thirty-three warships and transports carrying the first contingent to England, and to have had in 1S66 the honour of sheltering the convoy of His Royal Highness Prince Edward, afterwards King Edward VII. The people of this Gaspe peninsula, have contributed their mite to the upbuilding of Canada. They are prepared to continue to do their share in the future, and are asking only for fair treatment at the hands of parliament. I know the hon. member for Vancouver and his colleagues on the other side would be acting in accordance with the wishes of their political friends in those two constituencies if they would give consideration to this bill. We are simply asking that justice be done. The demand is not unreasonable and I hope there will be no further trouble and that the bill will be adopted. The manner in which these people have been treated has not been a credit to Canada, and I hope the house will allow the bill to pass.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in reference to this bill. .1 happen to know the Gaspe peninsula and the railway in question. I wish to repeat in the House of Commons what I said in the railway committee, namely, that I support the taking over of this railway. Why? This is a section of the country which is most at-

C.N.R.-Branch Bines
tractive, contains a fine population and, I believe, has a future. But in any case it is a large section which is not adequately served at the present time and I think, on the policy that we have been carrying out elsewhere throughout the Dominion, it is time that we gave a fairly good service to Gaspe. I have taken an interest in this area and the people there have waited patiently a long time. Therefore I have pleasure in supporting the bill.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
When this bill was before the railway committee we secured a good deal of information in regard to the history of the railway. The hon. member for Bona-venture just a few minutes ago gave the committee some information which is evidently a transcript of the address that Sir Henry Thornton delivered before the committee. I want to call attention to a very peculiar incident that occurred in the committee at that time. There is a record made by the reporters of the proceedings in connection with this bill in the railway committee. We have never before had any of the business of the railway committee recorded by the reporters this session or for many sessions past; but in view of the fact that Mr. Speaker and the hon. member for Bonaventure were very much interested in the acquisition of this line by the Canadian National Railways, no doubt Mr. Speaker took the opportunity of seeing to it that the reporters were present for the purpose of taking down the speeches delivered by Mr. Speaker and the hon. member for Bonaventure. That, of course, is not allowed to the ordinary member of the house; but, Mr. Speaker, being in a privileged position, took advantage of his privileges on this occasion. I want to protest against anything of that description being carried on. There is no question in my mind that Mr. Speaker and the hon. member for Bonaventure will have these speeches printed and broadcast. I do not know whether this will be done at the expense of the public or not, but the country will have to pay for the reporting staff in any case. These two hon. gentlemen will broadcast these speeches in their constituencies, naturally, for their own benefit. I merely make this statement that I object to anything of that description being carried on where certain members have privileges which other members do not secure. It is not fair.
Coming to the question of this railway, from the evidence given before the committee I am satisfied that it will be probably twenty years before this railway pays back a dollar of the capitalization. I aim not opposing the acquisition of this railway because I recognize
the fact that we have in Canada many sore spots for the healing of which we must make provision such as we are doing by this bill.
In the interests of the people of Canada as a whole and of confederation, the house must stretch its conscience sometimes in that regard.
There is another point that I want to bring before the committee, and it is this. If I understand the matter correctly, neither the Intercolonial nor the Transcontinental railway is included in the present capitalization of the Canadian National Railways; the Canadian National is not responsible for the capitalization of either of those two lines. Some two years ago we passed the Maritime Freight Rates Act for the purpose of taking care of the Canadian National in the maritime section, and also for the purpose of reducing freight rates to the extent of 20 per cent of the rates in force at that particular time. I opposed that proposal then because I thought it was poor economics, but in view of the fact that the house finally passed the legislation,
I accept that as the best judgment of the * house and I am quite willing to support the principle now. But as regards this railway and the next three which are on the order paper, not one of them will be a paying proposition. We cannot hope that for some time to come these four lines will pay even the actual running expenses.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: How soon does my hon. friend expect the Hudson Bay railway to pay?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
The Hudson Bay railway will, I hope, pay its way within five years, but let me point out to my hon. friend that it is in a very similar position to these and I will explain my position in regard to it a little later on. A moment ago I stated that I do not believe these four lines, taking them as a whole, will pay their wray for many years to come. That means that the country will have to pay the losses incurred by the Canadian National Railways under the Maritime Freight Rates Act in connection with these four railways. But, as I stated before,
I maintain that these districts are sore spots, and if this house can heal those sore spots, it is our duty to do so.
Another point of importance is that under this legislation the capitalization of these lines will be charged up against the Canadian National and I protest against that procedure.
If you are going to buy these railways, then buy them out of moneys provided by the treasury of the country. It is not fair to load up our national system with a number of deadhead railway? and then expect the

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
national system to make enough money to pay the interest charges on the capital invested. In view of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, and in view of the fact that the Intercolonial railway and the Transcontinental railway are not charged up against the capitalization of the Canadian National, it is only fair that we should place these four railways on the same 'basis and relieve the Canadian National of the amount of their capitalization.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: My hon. friend is surely not clear there. The Maritime Freight Rates Act does just what he suggests should be done.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: But not so far as capitalization is concerned. The capitalization will be charged up against the Canadian National system.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Will the minister please explain the matter then?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: The interest upon the capital invested is a fixed charge which is taken into consideration in determining the payments to be made under the Maritime Freight Rates Act for the deficits incurred under the act.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: It takes care of the deficits.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Of the interest on the capital.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: If that is so, I am glad indeed to hear it, and so far as I am concerned, as long as these lines are not charged up against the capitalization of the Canadian National, I have no objection to the house taking this attitude towards these four lines, that, as I stated before, they are to all intents and purposes national problems which we have to solve, and so heal these sore spots.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Before we leave that point, may I ask the minister whether what he says is Correct? How is it that this line is included in those recited by Sir Henry Thornton as being part of the provision for capital expenditure next year? On page 117 of the report of the special committee, Sir Henry Thornton is reported as saying, enumerating certain things all of which I shall not read:
The Quebec, Oriental and Atlantic, Quebec Western Railway, $3,500,000.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
My hon. friend evidently did not understand my ansiwer to the hon. member for Acadia. Certainly the money requires to be raised to pay for these rail-

ways which we are now discussing, but the interest charge on that money from year to year becomes a fixed charge on a railway included within the area covered by the Maritime Freight Rates Act and, therefore, the interest charge upon the capital is not an ordinary charge upon the system as a whole but becomes a part of the deficit under the Maritime Freight Rates Act if a deficit exists from year to year.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
I understand from the
minister that the interest charges will become part and parcel of any deficit which will occur under the operation of the Maritime Freight Rates Act.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Will the original capital necessary to take over these lines be charged against the Canadian National railway system? Will it become part of their capital account? That is the point.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
I am not quite sure what my hon. friend has in mind. What I was anxious to provide was that the system as a whole should not be prejudiced nor placed in a more difficult position because parliament in its wisdom, or lack of it, out of its desire to heal these sore spots to which my hon, friend referred, decided to do a certain thing. So far as that phase of it is concerned, the Maritime Freight Rates Act undoubtedly covers the point because the interest charge is part of the fixed charge and becomes part of the deficit which is made up annually by a vote of this parliament. So far as the whole capital structure of the Canadian National railways is concerned, most certainly all sums represented by actual physical assets are included therein, and I do not think that there can be any exception taken to that.
With reference to the criticisms, my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre made a perfectly understandable criticism on the basis of an economic report made in connection with this line by the Director of Economics who is now Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals and one of the engineers of the Canadian National railway system. I would point out to my hon. friend in that connection that economic surveys, of which this was merely one, were made in connection with all of the lines writh which we are dealing in the various bills before the house, and my hon. friend will find the particular comment to which he made reference in the reports on others of these lines as well as the one presently under discussion.
As I said yesterday in connection with these matters, we are linked with the past, and we

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
are dealing with these matters because we are linked with the past, and .because the past carries with it certain obligations. My hon. friend from Bonaventure has indicated to us some of the obligations which are involved in connection with the lines now under discussion and I am very glad, I may say, to be able to propose to parliament the carrying out of at least one of the pledges made by the Conservative party at the last election. If I can help in that particular, I am very glad to do so.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
The minister apparently
forgets that the county turned down the proposition.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend
should say that the county declined the bribe.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
The minister is scarcely
fair. From the reading of the document by the hon. member for Bonaventure it would appear that Mr. Meighen, who was then the leader of the party, stated that the matter would be given sympathetic consideration. He made no pledge, and my hon. friend knows '.hat.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
But his candidate in that constituency', one of his ministers, a member of the Privy Council of Canada, speaking with all the authority attached to his cabinet position, said:	If this road is not taken over
in two years, I will have to resign.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: He did not resign.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: He never got the opportunity.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Since the minister used the word " bribe," does he consider this a bribe at the present time?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
No, and I regret having
used that word, although I used it only in a good-humoured sense. It is quite proper for a political party to give indications to the electorate with regard to any policy which it proposes to put into effect. I regret having used the word. It is not usual for me to use language like that. It is rather more characteristic of some hon. gentlemen I see on the other side.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Of whom, for example?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
"A political bribe" is
not infrequently used by hon. gentlemen opposite in argument.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Suppose we get on with the discussion.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
I have only this to say,
particularly to my hon. friend from Acadia. I think it would be fair in dealing with a 78594-161
matter of this kind to imagine the condition of the Gaspe peninsula without a railway at all. It is easy to conceive of it as a similar area in western Canada, and I venture to say that my hon. friend from Acadia, with those around him, would be one of the first to support a proposal to build a line into such an area containing the resources and population which this area contains. Looked at from that point of view, we are getting a line of railway which conservatively is worth as much as a new branch line.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Physically, yes. My hon. friends cannot at one time use the report of the experts when they desire to criticize, and then refuse to accept that same report in regard to intrinsic values. At any rate, we are getting this property at $17,500 per mile. Will any of my hon. friends stand up and say that we could build a branch line of the lowest standard for anything like $17,500 per mile?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: That is not the point at issue. The point is whether these lines will pay or not. We expect that a branch line in western Canada will pay and the railway companies say that they will not build unless they can see profits ahead. That is the attitude that Sir Henry Thornton takes in regard to a number of branch lines in western Canada right now.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
If we would only put
ourselves in the position of thinking of this great peninsula without any railway at all, I know that my hon. friend would be one of those who would argue that a railway into an area possessing such resources and such population would pay, and I would honour him for it. I am adopting the position that if there were no railway there, then this parliament would undoubtedly be willing to authorize the construction of one, and to build one would cost twice as much as we are spending to buy the one already there. I am not in a position to say that this railway will pay, but I have sifficient faith in the Canadian National organization to know that they can bring about quite an improvement in the traffic returns of that railway by applying to the development of the peninsula which it serves the power of a great organization both in the development of trade, in the development of tourist traffic, and in the development of manufactures.
It is difficult, Mr. Chairman, to deal with these old matters. When the provinces of Canada met with the Dominion government in Ottawa, province after province raised

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

these railway problems, not from the point of view of their economic soundness as proper acquisitions for the Canadian National railway or the Dominion government, but from the point of view of their historical connection and the obligations in a Dominion sense attaching to them. The Dominion government undertook as a matter of policy that the Canadian National management should be asked to look into these various situations and, if possible, to negotiate ways of dealing with them. May I point out to the committee that if the Gaspe railway had happened to be owned by Mackenzie and Mann in 1918 instead of by the poor shareholders of the defunct Charing Cross bank, it would to-day have been a part of the national system, and there would not have been a word of complaint about it, but because the owners happened to be the poor shareholders of the defunct Charing Cross bank instead of Mackenzie and Mann, this railway was left outside.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Does the minister think that Mackenzie and Mann would ever have constructed that road?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mackenzie and Mann
constructed many a railroad1 through less promising territory than the Gaspe peninsula, and my hon. friend can think of some instances himself if he will reflect for a moment or two. The point is, after all, we have these railway sore spots. They have been there for years. The file in the Department of Railways and Canals relating to the Gaspe peninsula is a foot thick and goes back pretty well to confederation. The ministers of railways back as far as Sir Charles Tupper helped to promote it, and I think we are doing a good thing for Canada, and we are not harming the Canadian National system in the slightest degree by including these lines within the terms of the Maritime Rates Act.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: I do not know whether the minister intended it or not, but I am afraid he did put me in a wrong light. The minister knows very well that I did not object to the buying of this railway.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Quite so.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: I thought possibly some of his remarks might carry the implication that I objected to its purchase.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
I said I supported the
purchase on general principles for the benefit of Canada. I have nothing further to say so long as the Canadian National system is protected.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as a member of the railway committee which had this bill under consideration, I feel that having considered it very carefully, with practically all the information now submitted to the house before that committee, I must follow the course I then pursued, that is, approve this bill. But I think the Minister of Railways cannot contend for a moment that this is a good business buy. The railway will not pay within any reasonable time that we can anticipate. It is a more or less decrepit railway, old fashioned in its weight of rails, in its bridges, trestles, structures, and equipment.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
What is the weight
of rail?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Sixty pounds to the yard,
whereas they are now putting in one hundred pound rails.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Not on branch lines.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: From eighty to one hundred pounds. However that may be, the cost of reproduction to-day is the cost of the physical reproduction, less depreciation accrued over the years since the lines were first put in place. But that does not take into account the conditions I have referred to, the inadequate, obsolescent-or whatever you may call it-condition of the railway to say nothing of its not having been kept in proper repair. Sir Henry Thornton says it will cost $147,000 to patch the railway up so that it may take care of the present traffic.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
My hon. friend is very
close as to the amount, but my understanding of Sir Henry Thornton's statement is that it would require that sum to bring the railway u,p to normal branch line standard.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
We need not quarrel about
that. It is simply bringing up to branch line standard a railway that does not handle a great deal of traffic anyway. I do not think it is any use for the minister to attempt to take any comfort in the reflection that we are building branch lines in the western provinces that may not pay on their actual construction cost. Those branch lines fit into the system as a whole and contribute to the general traffic. I do not think we can get very far by comparing this acquisition with a new branch line constructed in the western provinces. But I think the minister is on sound ground when he says there is some obligation on us to take this road over viewing it from this other angle, that we should not forget the frank statement of the railway officials concerned, that in buying the road we are relieving the English bondholders to some

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
extent of an obligation which this country was under to them for financing the railway. This factor had a good deal of influence on my judgment. Now, there has been in times past- a lot of criticism on the part of English investors of Canadian financial methods, and it is not thought by Sir Henry Thornton, and I judge by the minister and. others associated with him, to be advisable to incur any more of such criticism. There is no doubt that if we sat tight on this proposition and let the bondholders come to us, we could squeeze them down to a lower figure. But I am not complaining of the action of the railway officials in giving what under all the circumstances is a fair figure. I do not think it is the part of this government to wait for the road . to drop into our basket for practically no consideration at all. To my mind those two considerations are preeminent. One, that we have an obligation to these people. There is no good reason why we should leave the Gaspe peninsula out of our calculations. That obligation I think we should fulfil. The other consideration I have already adverted to, namely, the impression to be left upon English investors in regard to money which they have bona fide placed in a railway enterprise in Canada.
For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I think there is no doubt in our minds that we are buying as a matter of business what is a very bad business proposition, and certainly my vote was not influenced in committee at all by the supposition that we are getting a money making property. I think, as an toon, member expressed it, it is about one of the worst things we have ever been obliged to do, but we have to do it. That expresses the opinion of many members in regard to this matter. I find no fault with the government for yielding to pressure, if it can be called pressure, for the reasons I have outlined, but I cannot say they are justified in their action by any consideration of the dollars and cents involved in the transaction.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Since the reports of the
experts of the Canadian National Railways was made I have received a letter from Mr. J. S. Gordon, general manager of these two railways, giving the returns for last year. Let me quote from his letter:
Our revenue for 1928 for the two railways was $609,240 with expenses of $548,910, leaving a net operating revenue of $60,330. Of course this balance of $60,330 is debited with such items as hire of equipment, taxes, etc., but in railway accounting, these items are regarded as non-operating expenses.
Mr. Gordon states that within the last twelve months considerable development has 78594-1611
taken place in the Gaspe peninsula. The Madawaska Corporation has gone in there and erected a mill which employs hundreds of men. They have leased a mill at Restigouche, and they have cut during the past winter 50,000,000 feet of lumber. So the traffic will increase with this steady development.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Everybody will be pleased
if that works out.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: In the centre of the peninsula, near Grand Cascapedia, there is a zinc and lead mine which has been declared by the geological survey here to be the equal of the Jobson deposits in Missouri, one of the richest of the kind in North America. For these reasons, and for the still greater reason that these people are entitled to fair treatment on a equal basis with all parts of Canada, I again urge that the house pass this bill.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: What is the relation between the fixed charges and the maritime freight rates? Why should those fixed charges be added to the maritime freight rates?

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Under the terms of the Maritime Freight Rates Act the deficit on all of the roads within that region are paid by a vote of this parliament to the Canadian National Railways. Now, the deficits are arrived at by taking the revenues and deducting them from the expenses including the fixed charges. The fixed charges in the area covered by the Maritime Freight Rates Act including interest on the bonds outstanding -as for instance, in connection with the Halifax and Southwestern railway-in fact interest on the outstanding bonds of any of the lines which are now part of the Canadian National system in that area is taken into account. If my memory serves me aright, there is no interest involved in connection with any portion of the Intercolonial railway, buit there are interest charges connected with parts of privately owned systems which come into the area in question. I fnentioned the Halifax and Southwestern as an instance of what I mean in that regard. This line and each one of the others which will come before the committee shortly will have fixed charges attaching to them. I do not claim that these roads, at least immediately, will be profitable to the Canadian National. By the terms of the Maritime Freight Rates Act this country as a whole bears the interest charge on the capital. The Canadian National Railways administer the property under the terms of the maritime rates act.
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Will not the minister admit that the interest on capital expenditure we are now authorizing amounting to some $3,500,000 will be simply carried in t'he Canadian National accounts, with the large interest charged on its total indebtedness to the government? It will not be segregated in any way.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
It will be segregated in
the accounts in accordance with the terms of the maritime rates act. That is to say, the Canadian National will receive from the Finance department, under the vote which is made each year under the maritime rates act, an amount equivalent to interest charge on the bonds against this particular property and against all other properties in the maritime rates area.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Paid out of a vote of the government.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: My understanding is that the Duncan report was in favour of a 20 per cent reduction in freight rates in certain areas in the maritime provinces. That reduction was made and became chargeable to the Dominion treasury. If that is right I cannot see the relation between that and interest on capital charge.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: I am not referring to the Duncan report, which is not legislation.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: I know.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
The legislation is the
maritime rates act.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Based on the report.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: It carries out the Duncan report. In placing that legislation before the house I carefully explained just the feature of it which is now under discussion. It was well understood and in succeeding sessions has been the subject of discussion when the estimates relating to it have arisen. The recommendation of the Duncan report in that connection is familiar to hon. members. It is provided that the cost of this relief shall be definitely borne by the Dominion government, who will make the necessary reimbursement to the Canadian National Railways without impairing the financial results of the operations of the system.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext:
That is the 20 per cent,
reduction.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: Yes. But there is somewhere-I cannot lay my finger on it at the moment-a reference to the machinery for working out the problem in the area in question.

maintopic: QUEBEC ORIENTAL AND ATLANTIC, QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAYS
speechtext: It does not apply to this interest.

The house in committee on Bill No. 174, respecting Canadian National Railways and to authorize the acquisition of the Saint John and Quebec Railway-Mr. Dunning-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Authority to purchase St. John and Quebec Railway.
Mr. MaoLAREN:	When the Transcontinental was built it was run diagonally across the province of New Brunswick, terminating at Moncton, which is an inland town. The Transcontinental therefore gave no direct access to the sea-an indirect access, it is true, but not the shortest nor nearly the shortest route that could be selected. Consequently the province of New Brunswick felt that the Transcontinental did not afford a sufficiently direct outlet to the sea for transportation and therefore proceeded to have constructed this railway which is called the St. John and Quebec Railway. It was built down to the valley of the St. John river, a valley very well known to the country as fertile for both fruit and grain. This railway was partly built in 1914, when the war broke out; then difficulties arose. The government did not wish to proceed with any railway construction beyond what was absolutely essential, and work on this line ceased. The original idea was that the railway should run from St. John and join the Transcontinental at Grand Falls, but this involved the construction of two bridges and at the request of the Dominion government the plan was modified and resulted in the construction of a railway from Centreville to Westfield, so that while the railway is called the St. John and Quebec railway it does not touch either St. John or Quebec; it is suspended between the two, as it were.

Like Mahomet's coffin.
C.N.R.-Refunding Obligations

That is the present
situation, but it will be changed in future if the government follow this idea. I would like hon. members of the house, including my hon. friend the leader of the group to my left, to look at this not as a deadend railway but as one with a promising future.
How soon?

Just as soon as the
government decides to carry out this program by extending the railway eighteen miles further into St. John and on to Grand Falls. Then we will have transcontinental transshipments of grain to the port of St. John, which is a very large item. The minister need not shake his head.

I did not shake my
head; I merely looked surprised.

I will not delay the
house except to say that this was the original idea, and I believe it will persist. The faith of the whole province was behind the construction of this railway; they considered that the plans were based on solid ground, and I am of the same opinion. It was because of the war and at the request of the Dominion government that the railway was not completed, but it is still active; it passes through numerous towms and a great deal of construction will not be required to finish the work. When that is done the government can send grain over its own lines by a shorter route than is available to-day. This bill will afford relief to the province of New Brunswick because it will enable the Canadian National Railways to take over a line which the province has not felt able to complete.
Carried.
I second the motion.
